Apple___Apple_scab.summary: A common apple disease that spreads in cool, wet weather. It weakens trees and makes fruit scabby and cracked.
symptoms: Olive-green to brown, velvety spots on leaves that later turn black
Spotted leaves turn yellow and fall early
Dark, rough, corky scabs on the fruit
actions: Pick off badly spotted leaves and clear fallen leaves and fruit from under the tree
Prune crowded branches so leaves dry faster after rain
In wet weather, protect new leaves with a fungicide labeled for apple scab (e.g. captan, sulfur, or mancozeb where allowed)
prevention: Plant scab-resistant apple varieties
Clear all fallen leaves after the season: the fungus survives on them
Water at the base of the tree, not over the leaves

Apple___Black_rot.summary: A fungus that causes leaf spots, branch cankers and rotting fruit. It survives on dead wood and dried-up fruit.
symptoms: Small purple spots on leaves that grow into brown circles with a purple edge ("frogeye" spots)
Fruit rot that starts at the blossom end, turns black and shows rings
Sunken, reddish-brown cankers on branches
actions: Remove dried, mummified fruit from the tree and the ground
Prune out dead branches and cankers, cutting back into healthy wood, and burn or bury them
Apply a fungicide labeled for black rot (e.g. captan) during the growing season
prevention: Keep the orchard clean of dead wood and old fruit
Avoid wounding trees, and prune in dry weather
Keep trees vigorous with good watering and feeding

Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.summary: A rust fungus that needs two hosts: apple and juniper (red cedar). In spring, spores blow from galls on junipers to apple leaves.
symptoms: Bright yellow-orange spots on the top of leaves
Small black dots in the center of the spots
Tube-like or hair-like growths under the spots on the leaf underside
actions: Remove badly infected leaves
If junipers grow nearby, look for orange, jelly-like galls on them in wet weather and cut them off
Protect apple leaves from pink bud until after petal fall with a fungicide labeled for rust (e.g. myclobutanil)
prevention: Plant rust-resistant apple varieties
Do not plant apples near junipers or red cedars

Apple___healthy.summary: No signs of disease on this leaf.
actions: Keep checking leaves every week, on both sides
Act early if spots, powder, curling or yellowing appear
prevention: Prune in dry weather to let light and air into the tree
Remove fallen leaves and fruit, where diseases survive
Water the soil, not the leaves

Blueberry___healthy.summary: No signs of disease on this leaf.
actions: Keep checking leaves every week, on both sides
Act early if spots, powder, curling or yellowing appear
prevention: Keep the soil acidic and well drained, with mulch
Prune out old canes to keep bushes open
Water the soil, not the leaves
Blueberry___healthy.note: SmartCrop only learned what healthy blueberry leaves look like. It cannot detect blueberry diseases yet.

Cherry_(including_sour)___Powdery_mildew.summary: A fungus that grows as white powder on leaves and young shoots. Unlike most diseases, it spreads during warm, dry days with humid nights.
symptoms: White, powdery patches on leaves, often on the underside first
Young leaves curl, pucker or stay small
Powdery patches or rough, russeted skin on fruit
actions: Prune out heavily infected shoots
Remove water sprouts and suckers, which are usually infected first
Spray a product labeled for powdery mildew (e.g. sulfur or potassium bicarbonate) as soon as spots appear
prevention: Prune to keep the canopy open and airy
Avoid too much nitrogen fertilizer, which makes soft, easily infected growth
Plant less susceptible varieties

Cherry_(including_sour)___healthy.summary: No signs of disease on this leaf.
actions: Keep checking leaves every week, on both sides
Act early if spots, powder, curling or yellowing appear
prevention: Prune after harvest to keep the tree open
Remove fallen leaves and fruit
Water at the base and avoid wetting the leaves

Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.summary: A fungus that survives on old corn residue and spreads in warm, humid weather. Heavy infection before the grain fills can cut yield.
symptoms: Long, narrow, rectangular gray to tan spots
Spot edges are straight because they stop at the leaf veins
Spots start on lower leaves and move up; leaves can die early
actions: Check how far up the plant the spots have reached
If spots reach the upper leaves around tasseling, a fungicide labeled for gray leaf spot (e.g. a strobilurin or triazole) can protect yield
Ask your agriculturist whether spraying pays off for your field
prevention: Plant resistant hybrids
Rotate with a crop other than corn for at least one season
Bury or remove infected corn residue after harvest

Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.summary: A common rust fungus spread by wind. It usually causes little yield loss on field corn, but it can hurt sweet corn and susceptible hybrids.
symptoms: Small, oval, cinnamon-brown powdery bumps (pustules) on both sides of the leaf
Pustules turn dark brown to black later in the season
Heavily infected leaves turn yellow and dry
actions: Watch whether the rust spreads to the upper leaves
Spraying is rarely needed; consider a fungicide labeled for rust only for sweet corn or heavy infection before tasseling
prevention: Plant rust-resistant hybrids
Plant early so the crop matures before rust builds up

Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.summary: A fungus favored by mild temperatures and long periods of wet leaves from dew or rain. It survives on corn residue.
symptoms: Long, cigar-shaped gray-green to tan spots, 2.5 to 15 cm long
Spots appear first on the lower leaves
Dark, dusty spores can form on the spots in humid weather
actions: Check whether the spots are moving to the upper leaves
If spots reach the upper leaves before or at tasseling, a fungicide labeled for northern leaf blight can protect yield
Ask your agriculturist whether spraying pays off for your field
prevention: Plant resistant hybrids
Rotate away from corn for at least one season
Bury or remove infected residue

Corn_(maize)___healthy.summary: No signs of disease on this leaf.
actions: Keep checking leaves every week, on both sides
Act early if spots, rust bumps or streaks appear
prevention: Rotate corn with other crops
Remove or bury crop residue after harvest
Plant hybrids resistant to the diseases common in your area

Grape___Black_rot.urgencyNote: In warm, wet weather it can destroy most of the berries. Protect the vines now.
Grape___Black_rot.summary: A fungus that attacks leaves, shoots and berries. Infected berries shrivel into hard, black "mummies" that carry the disease into the next season.
symptoms: Small, round, reddish-brown spots on leaves with a dark border
Tiny black dots inside the spots
Berries turn brown, then shrivel into hard, black mummies
actions: Remove mummified berries and infected leaves from the vine and the ground, and destroy them
Prune out infected shoots
Protect new growth until a few weeks after bloom with a fungicide labeled for black rot (e.g. mancozeb or myclobutanil)
prevention: Clean up all mummies and prunings before new growth starts
Train and prune vines so air moves through the canopy
Choose a sunny site

Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).summary: A long-term trunk disease caused by several wood-rotting fungi that enter through pruning wounds. There is no cure; good pruning limits its spread.
symptoms: "Tiger stripe" leaves: yellow or reddish-brown bands between the veins that dry out
Small, dark spots on the berries
Sometimes a whole vine wilts and dies suddenly in hot weather
actions: Mark affected vines and cut out dead or discolored wood well below the visible damage
Remove and burn badly affected vines and all prunings
Disinfect pruning tools between vines
prevention: Prune in dry weather and protect large pruning cuts with a wound sealant
Keep pruning cuts small and avoid big wounds on old wood
Use healthy planting material from a trusted nursery

Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.summary: A leaf spot fungus that appears late in the season in warm, humid areas and can make leaves fall early.
symptoms: Irregular, dark red-brown to black spots on leaves
Spots grow together and the leaf dries out
Leaves drop early
actions: Remove and destroy infected leaves
Thin the leaves around the grape clusters so air can move
Fungicides used against other grape diseases (e.g. mancozeb or copper) usually control it too
prevention: Clean up fallen leaves
Prune for an open canopy
Avoid overhead watering

Grape___healthy.summary: No signs of disease on this leaf.
actions: Keep checking leaves every week, on both sides
Act early if spots, powder, stripes or yellowing appear
prevention: Prune for an open, airy canopy
Remove fallen leaves, prunings and old berries
Water the soil, not the leaves

Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).urgencyNote: No cure, and the insect that spreads it can carry it to nearby trees. Get it confirmed by your agriculture office quickly.
Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).summary: One of the most serious citrus diseases. A bacterium spread by the Asian citrus psyllid, a tiny insect, blocks the tree's food flow. Trees decline and fruit becomes small, lopsided and bitter.
symptoms: Blotchy yellow mottling that looks different on the left and right halves of the leaf
Yellow shoots on part of the tree
Small, lopsided fruit that stays green at the bottom and tastes bitter
actions: Ask your Municipal Agriculture Office or the Bureau of Plant Industry to confirm it; only a lab test is certain
If confirmed, remove the infected tree to protect the rest of the orchard
Control psyllids on the remaining trees with sprays labeled for psyllids
prevention: Plant only certified disease-free seedlings
Check new shoots regularly for psyllids
Coordinate psyllid control with neighboring farms
Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).note: For orange, SmartCrop only learned this one disease and no healthy orange leaves, so it may label any orange leaf this way. Never cut down a tree based on this app alone.

Peach___Bacterial_spot.summary: A bacterial disease spread by rain and wind. It is worst in sandy soils and in windy, wet weather.
symptoms: Small, angular, purple to brown spots on leaves
Spot centers fall out, leaving "shot holes"
Leaves turn yellow and drop; fruit gets small dark spots and cracks
actions: Remove badly infected leaves and twigs
Copper sprays labeled for peach can help early in the season; use them carefully, since copper can burn peach leaves
Avoid working among wet trees, which spreads the bacteria
prevention: Plant resistant varieties
Use windbreaks to reduce wind-blown rain
Keep trees healthy, but avoid too much nitrogen

Peach___healthy.summary: No signs of disease on this leaf.
actions: Keep checking leaves every week, on both sides
Act early if spots, holes, curling or yellowing appear
prevention: Prune to an open center to let air in
Remove fallen leaves and fruit
Water at the base of the tree

Pepper_bell___Bacterial_spot.summary: A bacterial disease spread by splashing water, wet hands and tools, and infected seed. It is worst in warm, rainy weather.
symptoms: Small, water-soaked spots on leaves that turn brown, often with a yellow edge
Spotted leaves turn yellow and drop
Raised, scabby spots on the fruit
actions: Remove infected leaves and badly infected plants
Do not touch or work among the plants while they are wet
Copper-based sprays (often mixed with mancozeb) can slow the spread
prevention: Use certified disease-free seed and seedlings
Rotate away from pepper and tomato for 2 to 3 years
Use drip watering or water at the base, not over the leaves

Pepper_bell___healthy.summary: No signs of disease on this leaf.
actions: Keep checking leaves every week, on both sides
Act early if spots, curling or yellowing appear
prevention: Use clean seed and seedlings
Rotate peppers with crops outside the tomato family
Water at the base and keep leaves dry

Potato___Early_blight.summary: A common fungus that attacks older leaves first, especially on stressed plants. It lowers yield when leaves die early.
symptoms: Dark brown spots with rings inside, like a target
A yellow area around the spots
Starts on older, lower leaves and moves up
actions: Remove badly infected lower leaves
Spray a fungicide labeled for early blight (e.g. chlorothalonil or mancozeb) when spots appear
Keep plants well fed and watered so they resist infection
prevention: Rotate away from potato and tomato for at least 2 years
Use certified seed potatoes
Remove plant debris after harvest

Potato___Late_blight.urgencyNote: Act today. In cool, wet weather it can destroy a whole field within days and spread to neighboring farms.
Potato___Late_blight.summary: The disease behind the Irish potato famine. It spreads fast through airborne spores in cool, humid weather and also rots the tubers.
symptoms: Pale green, water-soaked patches on leaves that quickly turn brown or black
White, fuzzy growth on the leaf underside in humid weather
Brown, firm rot on the tubers
actions: Remove infected plants right away and destroy them; do not compost them
Spray the rest of the field with a fungicide labeled for late blight (e.g. mancozeb, chlorothalonil, or a systemic product such as cymoxanil or metalaxyl)
Tell nearby farmers so they can protect their crops
prevention: Plant certified, disease-free seed potatoes
Hill soil over the tubers to protect them
Destroy volunteer potatoes and piles of discarded potatoes

Potato___healthy.summary: No signs of disease on this leaf.
actions: Keep checking leaves every week, on both sides
Act fast if dark, water-soaked patches appear, especially in cool, wet weather
prevention: Use certified seed potatoes
Rotate potatoes with unrelated crops
Hill up soil and keep leaves dry when watering

Raspberry___healthy.summary: No signs of disease on this leaf.
actions: Keep checking leaves every week, on both sides
Act early if spots, powder, curling or yellowing appear
prevention: Remove old canes after they have fruited
Keep rows narrow so air can move
Water at the base
Raspberry___healthy.note: SmartCrop only learned what healthy raspberry leaves look like. It cannot detect raspberry diseases yet.

Soybean___healthy.summary: No signs of disease on this leaf.
actions: Keep checking leaves every week, on both sides
Act early if spots, rust bumps or yellowing appear
prevention: Rotate soybean with corn or other crops
Plant disease-resistant varieties
Use clean, good-quality seed
Soybean___healthy.note: SmartCrop only learned what healthy soybean leaves look like. It cannot detect soybean diseases yet.

Squash___Powdery_mildew.summary: A very common fungus on squash, pumpkin and cucumber. It drains the plant, so fruit ripens poorly.
symptoms: White, powdery spots on leaves and stems
Spots spread until the whole leaf looks dusted with flour
Leaves turn yellow, then brown and dry
actions: Remove the most infected leaves
Spray a product labeled for powdery mildew, such as sulfur, potassium bicarbonate or neem oil
Cover the undersides of the leaves too
prevention: Plant resistant varieties
Give plants full sun and space for air to move
Remove plant debris after harvest
Squash___Powdery_mildew.note: For squash, SmartCrop only learned this one disease and no healthy squash leaves, so it may label any squash leaf this way. Check for the white powder yourself.

Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.summary: A fungus that spots and dries strawberry leaves, weakening plants and reducing next season's crop.
symptoms: Many small, irregular purple spots on the leaves
Spots join together and the leaf looks burned or scorched
Leaf edges dry and curl up
actions: Remove and destroy infected leaves
After harvest, cut back old leaves and clear them away
Use a fungicide labeled for leaf scorch (e.g. captan) if it keeps spreading
prevention: Plant resistant varieties and clean, certified plants
Use drip watering instead of overhead sprinklers
Space plants for good airflow and replant beds every few years

Strawberry___healthy.summary: No signs of disease on this leaf.
actions: Keep checking leaves every week, on both sides
Act early if spots, powder or yellowing appear
prevention: Use clean, certified plants
Mulch to keep fruit and leaves off the soil
Water at the base, in the morning

Tomato___Bacterial_spot.summary: A bacterial disease spread by splashing water, hands, tools and infected seed. It is worst in warm, wet weather.
symptoms: Small, dark, greasy-looking spots on leaves, sometimes with a yellow edge
Spots merge, and leaves turn yellow and drop
Small, raised, scabby spots on green fruit
actions: Remove infected leaves and badly infected plants
Do not touch or work among the plants while they are wet
Copper-based sprays (often mixed with mancozeb) can slow the spread
prevention: Use certified disease-free seed and seedlings
Rotate away from tomato and pepper for 2 to 3 years
Stake plants and water at the base

Tomato___Early_blight.summary: One of the most common tomato diseases. It starts on older leaves and can strip plants of leaves, exposing the fruit to sunscald.
symptoms: Brown spots with target-like rings on older leaves
Yellowing around the spots
Dark, sunken spots on stems and near the fruit stem
actions: Remove infected lower leaves and take them out of the garden
Mulch the soil to stop spores splashing up onto leaves
Spray a fungicide labeled for early blight (e.g. chlorothalonil, mancozeb or copper)
prevention: Rotate away from tomato, potato and eggplant for 2 to 3 years
Stake plants and prune lower leaves for airflow
Water at the base, in the morning

Tomato___Late_blight.urgencyNote: Act today. In cool, wet weather it can kill plants within days and spread to nearby tomato and potato farms.
Tomato___Late_blight.summary: A fast-spreading disease favored by cool, wet weather. It kills leaves and stems and rots the fruit.
symptoms: Large, irregular, greasy gray-green spots on leaves that turn brown
White, fuzzy growth on the leaf underside in humid weather
Firm, brown, greasy patches on the fruit
actions: Remove infected plants right away and bag or bury them; do not compost them
Protect the remaining plants with a fungicide labeled for late blight (e.g. mancozeb, chlorothalonil or cymoxanil)
Warn nearby tomato and potato growers
prevention: Keep leaves dry by watering at the base
Do not plant tomatoes next to potatoes
Use resistant varieties where available

Tomato___Leaf_Mold.summary: A fungus of humid conditions, especially greenhouses and tightly spaced plants. It rarely affects the fruit but lowers yield.
symptoms: Pale green or yellow spots on the upper side of leaves
Olive-green to brown, velvety mold under the same spots
Leaves wither and drop
actions: Improve ventilation and lower the humidity around plants
Remove infected leaves
Spray a fungicide labeled for leaf mold (e.g. chlorothalonil or copper) if it keeps spreading
prevention: Space and prune plants for airflow
Water at the base and avoid wetting the leaves
Use resistant varieties

Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.summary: A very common leaf spot fungus that spreads by splashing water. Severe cases strip the plant of its leaves.
symptoms: Many small, round spots with dark brown edges and gray or tan centers
Tiny black dots inside the spots
Starts on lower leaves, which turn yellow and fall
actions: Remove infected lower leaves
Mulch to stop soil splashing onto the leaves
Spray a fungicide labeled for Septoria leaf spot (e.g. chlorothalonil, mancozeb or copper)
prevention: Rotate away from tomatoes for at least a year
Remove weeds in the tomato family, such as nightshade
Clean up plant debris after harvest

Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.summary: Not a disease, but tiny pests that suck sap from the leaves. They multiply fast in hot, dry weather.
symptoms: Tiny yellow or white specks (stippling) on the leaves
Leaves turn bronze, dry out and fall
Fine webbing on the underside of leaves
actions: Spray the undersides of the leaves with a strong stream of water
Use insecticidal soap, neem or horticultural oil, covering the leaf undersides
If severe, use a miticide labeled for tomato, and switch products between sprays
prevention: Water plants regularly; drought-stressed plants attract mites
Control weeds where mites live
Avoid broad-spectrum insecticides that kill the mites' natural enemies

Tomato___Target_Spot.summary: A fungus of warm, humid climates. It looks a lot like early blight and can also spot the fruit.
symptoms: Brown spots with light-brown rings and a yellow edge
Spots merge and leaves fall
Small, sunken dark spots on the fruit
actions: Remove infected lower leaves and improve airflow
Spray a fungicide labeled for target spot (e.g. chlorothalonil, mancozeb or azoxystrobin)
Avoid working among wet plants
prevention: Rotate crops and remove plant debris
Avoid overhead watering
Do not plant too densely

Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.urgencyNote: No cure. Whiteflies carry it to nearby plants, so act before it spreads.
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.summary: A virus spread by whiteflies. Plants infected while young stay stunted and produce little fruit.
symptoms: Leaves curl upward and become small and cupped
Yellow leaf edges and yellowing between the veins
Stunted plants that drop flowers and set few fruits
actions: Pull out infected plants, bagging them first to trap whiteflies, and destroy them
Control whiteflies with yellow sticky traps and insecticidal soap or neem; use products labeled for whiteflies if there are many
Check nearby plants for whiteflies and the same symptoms
prevention: Plant TYLCV-resistant varieties
Raise seedlings under insect-proof net
Remove weeds that host whiteflies, and avoid planting next to infected fields

Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.urgencyNote: No cure. It spreads easily on hands and tools, so handle infected plants last.
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.summary: A very stable virus that spreads by touch, tools and seed. It can survive for months on surfaces and in plant debris.
symptoms: Light and dark green mottled (mosaic) pattern on the leaves
Distorted, curled or fern-like leaves
Stunted plants and unevenly ripening fruit
actions: Remove infected plants and destroy them
Wash hands with soap and disinfect tools after touching infected plants
Work on healthy plants first and infected areas last
prevention: Use resistant varieties and certified seed
Do not use tobacco products while handling plants
Remove plant debris after the season

Tomato___healthy.summary: No signs of disease on this leaf.
actions: Keep checking leaves every week, on both sides
Act early if spots, curling, mottling or yellowing appear
prevention: Stake plants and remove lower leaves that touch the soil
Water at the base and mulch the soil
Rotate tomato with crops outside the tomato family
